questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: An institution in high regard within my field of interest as well as a tradition for international cooperation. I wanted to get a feel for the advancements and prospects in the field in order to decide if I wanted to devote my career to its pursuits. Finally I wanted a place with an interesting and different culture and an opportunity to try and find my feet in that.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: As I was only there for 6 months, I didn't invest time in learning the native tongue prior to my stay. I hind sight this was a mistake that let to some social difficulties. The institution and administration around it was overall excellent.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Very easy - the administration was always very helpful and easy to get in touch with

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I received several e-mails with important information about what, when and how, in order to get set up in my new surroundings.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I succeded, but overall it is pretty difficult! The university provided a spot on an 'acute' waiting list in exchange for 400 €. This didn't guarantee me a place to live, but luckily there was one available for me. If a future student doesn't manage to find housing before start of the semester, I highly recommend to post-bone the trip altogether, as finding housing on-sight is almost impossible!!

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: If you do find a place it will almost certainly be close to campus with very nice facilities. If you don't find something before semester start, then abort or post-bone the trip, as finding housing on-sight is almost impossible!!

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Facilities are very fine and you're almost guaranteed to live very close to campus, but you have to build social- and practical/everyday circles yourselves. Where I lived, there was no common room or traditions a priori, but if you work for it then it should be possible to live very pleasantly.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I registered for a pre-planned semester called 'a minor', which contained a selection of 7 courses of a total 30 ECTS - the registration for these happened all at once, and so I only needed to register for the exams as they came along

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The administration was always very helpful and available - both in person and per e-mail.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all the courses I wanted and so there were no issues. I do not know however, if this generally applies outside the pre-planned 'minor'-structure.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Register as much in advance as possible. Additionally, for some reason students are not automatically signed up for the exams when registering for the course - they have to do that manually 6 weeks before the examination date. Remember to do that! Or ideally just do it at the first day of the courses - you might be forced to do a re-sit or take the exam on reduced time if you forget the deadline.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The university was a technical university and so I felt that the importance rested more on being able to apply, not necessarily understand - at least not in a deductive sense. Furthermore, the courses were held across faculties (physics, math, computer science, electro engineers, etc.) and so the level of theory was restricted to a 'lowest common denominator'. If one sought a deep theoretical understanding of the field, I would therefore say that the level was quite low. However, what they set out to do was the cultivate interdisciplinary cooperation and a broad understanding of the field, and that I think they succeded with quite nicely.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Much more 'Here are the general results, derived in a hand wavy manner, now go and apply them' as opposed to the approach at UCPH which I personally feel is more rooted in students understanding the 'why/how' and the capability to derive theory themselves. I think the difference rests on the institution being a technical university with close ties to the industry, which is fine, but something to keep in mind.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
I was enrolled in the minor "Quantum Science and Quantum Information" of 30 ECTS total spanning over a semester. The sub-courses included:

- TN3105   Mathematics for Quantum Physics
- TN3126   Information and Computation
- TN3166-A Semiconductor Quantum Bits
- TN3166-B Superconductor Quantum Bits
- TN3145   Quantum Communication and Computation
- TN3156   Quantum Sensing and Measurement
- TN3175   Quantum Engineering Group Project

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I think this package is recommendable to anyone wishing an overview of the current field of quantum computation and information - given that one is interested in the interdisciplinary more engineer-like approach of things. If you want to understand theory on a deep level (as a physicist), this is not programme for you :)

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Mostly events or going on bigger trips.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Food was generally cheaper than in DK - I especially noticed avocados, nuts, beer and coffee(!)
To eat out on a restaurant however was kind of expensive, but where isn't it? ;)

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: The university has what I would describe as a sports/crea -city next to it called 'X'. For an annual subscribtion you get access to every sport, dance form, martial arts, meditation, yoga, spinning, drawing, music -class - you name it! Additionally many of the more competitive associations in the city (swimming, rowing, sailing) are under the umbrella of X and so generally cheaper that elsewhere. Social events are arranged both by X but also volunteer student associations at or around campus. For instance they have a very serious/popular culture of sorority houses with rituals, uniforms, etc. as you picture it in american high school/college films.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Definitely subscribe to X, as it opens a lot of doors to try out many different sports, activities and events - athletic as well as creative. The sororities have a reputation of being pretty rough in their rituals (cutting the hair of new-comers or making them eat live fish etc.). I personally had a blast at the association DSZ Wave, which combines swimming, cycling and running for very low cost, with the opportunity to work out every day outside the weekend if that is what you wish. They have a great community and lots of social events/activities - no pre-history in either discipline is required. This is generally true for all the above - just go there!

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: I recommend to plan trips outside the home city - go see Haag, Rotterdam and Amsterdam, but also all the small cities around the country. Additionally I had great experience with using Flixbuses to visit the nearby countries (Germany, Belgium - even France) for a prolonged weekend.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Overall the culture was very easy to blend into. People are very friendly and ready to drag you along as a newcomer. However, if you want social interaction outside the community of international students, I highly recommend learning some Dutch! Not that people dont speak excellent english, but in large groups of Dutch people they quickly fall back to their native tongue (understandably), and then you quickly lose touch with the conversation. So do yourself a favor and learn at least something if you really want to get involved with the locals!

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Beer is a hit! As a general rule I would say: never say no to an invitation - always yes. It won't hurt you and you get to meet a lot of new people and try new stuff. Also try to be proactive yourself and invite people for lunch, coffee, movie night, whatever. The more you do this in the beginning, the better - otherwise you might quickly get into the habbit of just sticking with yourself...

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Maybe the alcohol culture is a little strong, but if you're form DK it shouldn't be too much of a chok. I never experienced a situation where I felt forced to drink beyond my limits though.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The friendliness and the importance of being a good host/guest (bring each other flowers and similar stuff)

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Get out of your apartment! Seek out students and associations - the sooner the better.
Sign up for X and try out something new each week!
Keep up with your studies, but remember all the other things in life. You are there for a limited amount of time - make sure you make the best of it.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Feeling capable - that it was in my power to take care of my self and build a life of studying, living and meeting people from scratch in a foreign country.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: To manage myself when things got rough or I was feeling down - you want to have a web of people and activities to keep you up and going, or chances are you might tend to isolate yourself in your room and jsut kill time untill you can go home again.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
